strengths: Novel and timely research question: exploring 2D Gaussian Splatting as an alternative visual substrate for CLIP-style vision-language alignment, moving beyond post-hoc token pruning toward inherently compact representations.

Solid systems-engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels with reported 90x fitting speedup and ~97% GPU utilization over prior open-source 2DGS implementations, which is a concrete and potentially reusable artifact for the community.
Reasonable set of algorithmic improvements (structured grid-based initialization, luminance-aware L1 pruning) that are individually validated with PSNR comparisons and visualizations (Fig. 3, 4).

The parameter-efficient adaptation strategy (reusing a frozen RGB-pretrained transformer backbone with a lightweight splat-aware stem and Perceiver resampler, training only ~7% of parameters) is a sensible and practical way to bootstrap a new modality without full pretraining.

Includes an informative negative/ablation result: training 2DGS encoders from scratch performs substantially worse than the adaptation approach, which is honestly reported and provides useful insight for future work.

Clear motivation grounded in real systemic issues (edge-cloud transmission costs, token explosion) and a well-organized related-work section situating 2DGS relative to INRs, codecs, and prior small-scale 2DGS classification work.
weaknesses: The central motivating claim (edge-cloud transmission/energy efficiency) is never empirically validated end-to-end: 2DGS fitting itself is an iterative per-image optimization process, and no latency/energy measurements are provided for encoding on edge hardware, which could offset or negate the claimed transmission savings; this is a significant gap given the paper's framing.

No comparison against simple, obvious baselines under matched compression budgets (e.g., downsampled/low-resolution RGB images, JPEG-compressed inputs, or existing token-reduction methods cited in Sec. 2) to establish that 2DGS is a better compressed substrate than trivial alternatives at equivalent bit/token budgets.

Reported compression ratios (3-23.5x) are computed from raw float16 splat parameters without applying the quantization pipeline the authors themselves cite (GaussianImage), so the practical/deployed compression advantage is overstated relative to what is actually demonstrated.

Scale is modest (12.8M DataComp subset, 38M-parameter vision encoder, RGB baseline only reaching 18.5% top-1 zero-shot) yet the paper repeatedly describes this as a "large-scale" study; conclusions about viability at true production scale (hundreds of millions of samples, larger backbones) remain unsupported extrapolations.

Absolute performance gap (13-15% vs 18.5% top-1) is presented positively, but given the already low RGB baseline ceiling, it is unclear whether the relative gap would persist, shrink, or grow at larger scale; no scaling-trend experiments (e.g., varying dataset size) are provided to support the claim of a promising trajectory.

Because the GS encoder reuses a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone, much of the achieved zero-shot accuracy is arguably attributable to the inherited RGB semantic representation rather than to the 2DGS input representation itself; the substantially worse from-scratch results (Fig. 7) reinforce this concern and complicate the claim that 2DGS is inherently a strong learnable substrate.

No code, checkpoints, or dataset splits are released at submission time (code is stated to be released "soon"), limiting reproducibility of both the CUDA kernel claims and the CLIP adaptation results.

Key quantitative claims (90x speedup, 97% GPU utilization, PSNR numbers) are reported without variance, multiple seeds, or details on how baselines were tuned, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported gains.

The energy-cost figures motivating the paper (0.1-0.2 kWh/GB mobile transmission, etc.) are taken from external industry reports rather than measured or connected quantitatively to the specific transmission savings achieved by the proposed pipeline, weakening the paper's own efficiency argument.

strengths: Novel and timely research question: is 2D Gaussian Splatting a viable compact visual substrate for CLIP-style vision-language alignment, addressing real edge-cloud bandwidth and token-explosion problems.

Solid systems/engineering contribution: batched CUDA kernels for 2DGS fitting achieving up to 90x speedup and ~97% GPU utilization, which is a meaningful practical enabler for large-scale GS-based pipelines.

Reasonably careful comparison methodology: width-matched RGB baseline (ViT-B/16 Small), token-count-matched comparisons (196 vs 98), and reporting both absolute and relative accuracy across 38 datasets.

Extensive ablation studies in the appendix (structured initialization, luminance-based pruning, distillation loss variants, stem architectures, normalization choices, hyperparameter sensitivity) that add credibility and insight into design decisions.
Transparent discussion of limitations, including the observation that GS performance is upper-bounded by the RGB teacher and is more sensitive to distribution shift.
Practical two-stage training recipe (RGB→GS distillation followed by lightweight CLIP adaptation) that is compute-efficient, training only ~10-14% of parameters.
weaknesses: The GS encoder relies on a frozen RGB-pretrained backbone and is explicitly distilled from RGB features, so the reported alignment quality is fundamentally bounded by and derivative of the RGB teacher; this weakens the central claim that 2DGS is an independent, self-sufficient multimodal substrate rather than a compressed proxy for RGB features.

The edge-cloud motivation is not fully supported: the paper does not analyze or discuss the feasibility/cost of fitting Gaussian splats on resource-constrained edge devices (fitting still takes seconds per batch even with heavy CUDA optimization on H100s), which is central to the claimed energy/bandwidth benefits.

No comparison against simpler compression baselines (e.g., low-resolution/downsampled RGB, JPEG at matched bitrate, or other lightweight codecs) to isolate whether the specific advantage comes from the Gaussian representation itself versus generic lossy compression.

Absolute zero-shot accuracy of the RGB baseline itself is quite low (~22% average across 38 datasets) due to the small-scale training setup (12.8M pairs, reduced-width ViT), raising concerns about whether trends observed here will hold at larger, more realistic CLIP training scales.

Evaluation is restricted to zero-shot classification; despite motivating the work with VLM token explosion and captioning-style pipelines, no generative/captioning or retrieval evaluation is provided to substantiate broader VLM applicability.

Reported compression ratios use uncompressed FP16 Gaussian parameters rather than the more aggressive quantization pipelines from prior GS compression work (e.g., GaussianImage), so real-world achievable compression may be less favorable than stated.

Methodological novelty relative to prior GS-based vision work (GaussianImage, LIG, GViT, GaussianToken) is mainly incremental (scaling + CLIP-specific adaptation) rather than introducing fundamentally new representational or architectural mechanisms.
Minor presentation issues, such as leftover placeholder text in citations (e.g., 'dblp.org dblp.org') and dense, hard-to-parse appendix figures without sufficient standalone explanation.
